1000746.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse Ullingsvangr, originally the name of the local rectory. The first element represents the genitive of Ullinn, a side form of Ullr (“Ull”) preserved primarily in place names; the second is vangr (“field, meadow; open grassy place”). The same divine-name element occurs in Ullensaker.
The municipality was established under the name Kinsarvik in 1837 and was renamed Ullensvang in 1870.

PIE word
 *né
Compound of fant (“vagrant, tramp”) + førkje (“girl, woman”), with linking -e- (“interfix”), literally “vagrant woman”.
The first component fant (“vagrant, tramp”) is from Old Norse fantr (“servant; itinerant person”), through Middle Low German from Italian fante (“boy, young man; servant, infantryman”), ultimately from Latin īnfāns (“speechless; infant, child”), composed of in- (“not”) and fāns (“speaking”), the present participle of for (“to speak, say”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *bʰeh₂- (“to speak, say”). The negative element ultimately continues Proto-Indo
